A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MUSHRA evaluation study and proposed variants. Their text, tables, figures, scoring formula, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions in v3.

before.justification: v1 reports original Hindi and Tamil listening experiments, including MUSHRA and CMOS scores, proposed-variant evaluations, and listener-sensitivity analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds English evaluations, objective-metric results, a participant survey, and further diagnostic analyses.

M1.justification: The NMR, DG, and combined procedures remain unchanged, including the six error counts, three perceptual dimensions, and scoring weights and caps. Section 5 newly describes iterative development, but the documented procedures and appendix guidelines do not establish a method revision.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates Hindi and Tamil using IndicTTS. v3 adds English systems trained on LJSpeech and evaluations by native US English speakers, substantially extending language, corpus, and listener-population coverage (Section 7).

E2.justification: Standard MUSHRA and CMOS remain the comparison protocols, with FS2, ST2, and VITS as the principal evaluated systems. XTTSv2 and duplicated VITS already appeared in v1's extended test; its table is moved into v3's main text. The new objective metrics assess alignment with conventional MUSHRA rather than introduce additional baselines against the proposed variants.

E3.justification: Table 1 increases DG panels from 14 Hindi and 15 Tamil listeners to 20 each, and DG-NMR panels from 15 to 20 each. New protocols include English evaluations with 30 listeners rating 30 utterances, English CMOS with 15 listeners, and a focused Tamil FS2-versus-VITS CMOS test. Section 4.7 also introduces PESQ, STOI, and SI-SDR measurements.

E4.justification: v3 adds objective-metric alignment analysis, CMOS-derived preference breakdowns, an 89-participant post-evaluation survey, and Tamil and English fault-isolation analyses (Section 4.7; Appendices A.2, A.5, A.7). A focused Tamil CMOS comparison investigates the FS2/VITS ranking discrepancy. Existing sensitivity, rejection-rule, and extended-system analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means, standard deviations, and 95% confidence intervals and use 1,000 subsampling trials for ranking sensitivity. v3 does not specify a revised uncertainty-estimation, seed, or significance-testing procedure. Larger listener panels and changed interval values affect settings and results.

E6.justification: DG and DG-NMR results are revised alongside the enlarged panels: Hindi DG-NMR ST2/VITS means change from 89.55/89.33 in v1 Table 4 to 84.97/85.68 in v3 Table 6, reversing their order. Original MUSHRA, CMOS, NMR, and extended-test scores are retained. v3 additionally reports English, objective-metric, preference, survey, and diagnostic results; these are added or revised findings, not same-setting TTS performance improvements.

T1.justification: The scoring formulas in v1 Appendix A.3 and v3 Appendix A.6 are algebraically identical. Reordering the arguments of min(7, SP) and changing notation or equation layout do not change the mathematics. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The central claims about reference-matching bias, judgement ambiguity, and the benefits of NMR/DG remain. The corpus contribution is revised from 47,100 ratings and 471 listeners to 246,000 Hindi/Tamil ratings and 492 listeners; Section 7 reports 255,000 annotations including English. These revise the stated contribution's scale without redefining its central scientific claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations for near-tied Tamil rankings and inflated anchor scores, discusses objective metrics' perceptual and language limitations, and uses survey responses to interpret rater behavior. Section 7 explicitly acknowledges no significant English variance reduction. Limitations now discuss missing demographics and additional biases, although Appendix A.8 inconsistently retains the statement that English was not evaluated.

D1.justification: v3 adds an explicit MANGO dataset-access link and identifies TorchAudio-Squim for objective measurements. It also documents rater demonstration calls, iterative guideline development, demographic nonresponse, and institutional ethics approval. XTTS training information is relocated rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v3 adds supporting literature on naturalness, expressive evaluation, anchor limitations, objective metrics, and perceptual biases, including Shirali-Shahreza and Penn, Merritt et al. (2018), Kumar et al. (2023a), and Zielinski. The existing positioning as a critique and refinement of MUSHRA remains.

P1.justification: v3 substantially expands explanatory material through a new MUSHRA background subsection and extended discussions of scoring and results. It adds dedicated English and Future Work sections and reorganizes the appendices, including moving the extended-test material into the main text. Much of the original introduction and method wording remains.

P2.justification: v3 adds objective-metric, English-comparison, and preference tables; a survey display; Tamil/English diagnostic plots; and English rating distributions. Several existing distribution plots are redrawn, Figure 5 is revised, and the extended-test table moves from the appendix to the main text. These changes substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: The English study directly addresses v1's explicit lack of English validation, while larger DG panels and targeted diagnostic analyses substantially strengthen assessment of the proposed protocols. Reporting the absence of significant English variance reduction also clarifies their limits. These gains outweigh incomplete editorial integration: Appendix A.8 still denies English evaluation, and Appendix A.5's 22% difficulty claim conflicts with Figure 9's 12% difficult plus 3% very difficult.
